passage:
Playschool note, Thursday (Ms Joyce, Butterfly group)
At drawing time Afreen had the only box of glitter crayons. Jagdish asked first, and she handed him two at once, saying, "You gave me your sticker yesterday." When Bittu reached for one, Afreen covered the box with both arms. "No. You never give me." Bittu sat down hard and sulked. I knelt between them and said, "Afreen remembers who shared. Bittu, what could you share today?" Bittu offered his blue clay. Afreen took it and slid one crayon across 🙂
Next step: a sharing song before drawing tomorrow.

qa.q: What had Jagdish given Afreen yesterday?
qa.a: Jagdish had given Afreen a sticker yesterday.

qa.q: What does Afreen covering the box with both arms show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she feels cross with Bittu, because in her mind he never shares with her.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms Joyce turned the moment around?
qa.a: Instead of ordering Afreen to share, Ms Joyce asked Bittu what he could share, and his blue clay opened the way to a crayon.

qa.q: What might it feel like for Bittu to hear "You never give me"?
qa.a: Bittu might feel stung and shut out, which is why he sits down hard and sulks until he finds a way to join in.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing the one who never does.

passage: Behind the rice fields, under the big guava tree, Reena, five, had filled her frock pocket with guavas. Joseph came running. Yesterday he had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond. Reena held out the biggest guava straight away. "For you. You gave me." Then Kuttan came, the boy who always kept his mango slices behind his back. "Give me one." Reena shook her head hard. "You don't give. I don't give." Kuttan kicked at the mud. Reena's Ammachi, drying chillies on a mat nearby, called out, "Kuttan, bring your mango tomorrow, and see what happens."

qa.q: What did Joseph share with Reena yesterday?
qa.a: He had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond.

qa.q: Why did Reena shake her head hard at Kuttan?
qa.a: She felt cross: in her mind Kuttan never shares, so he hadn't earned a guava: "You don't give. I don't give."

qa.q: What does Ammachi's suggestion offer Kuttan, and why might it work?
qa.a: It gives Kuttan a way to earn a turn by bringing his mango tomorrow, which fits the way Reena thinks about fairness 🙂

qa.q: How might Kuttan feel watching Joseph get the biggest guava?
qa.a: Kuttan might feel left out and cross, and perhaps start to notice that hiding his mango has a cost.

grounding: A young child gives her best guava to the friend who shared with her and refuses the boy who never shares.

passage: In the small park near their flats in Cape Town, Siddiq, five, was pushing his new red digger through the sand. Thabo wandered over. Last Saturday Thabo had let Siddiq ride Thabo's scooter all the way to the bench and back. "You can dig," Siddiq said, handing over the digger. Then Oliver from the swings came close, the boy who never let anyone touch his bucket. "My turn." Siddiq put a hand on the digger's scoop. "No. Thabo's turn. You never share your bucket." Oliver's face crumpled. On the bench, Siddiq's dad leaned forward. "What if Oliver lends the bucket?" Siddiq thought about it for a long time.

qa.q: What had Thabo let Siddiq ride last Saturday?
qa.a: Thabo had let Siddiq ride Thabo's scooter all the way to the bench and back.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq hand the digger to Thabo so quickly?
qa.a: He felt grateful for the scooter ride and thought Thabo deserved a turn back, like a fair swap.

qa.q: Was Dad's question a good way to handle the moment, and why?
qa.a: Yes; instead of forcing Siddiq to share, Dad offered Oliver a way into the "you give, I give" deal that Siddiq already believes in.

qa.q: How might Oliver see Siddiq's "You never share your bucket"?
qa.a: Oliver may feel hurt and surprised, perhaps realising for the first time that other children remember when he doesn't share.

grounding: A young child lends his toy to the friend who shared a scooter with him and refuses the child who never shares.

passage: In the office creche, Simran, five, had the animal puzzles. Kiran came over. Yesterday Kiran had given her the red crayon when she was colouring an apple. Simran pushed the box across at once. "You can do the lion. You gave me red." Then Babloo came, the boy who kept the blocks under his mat every day. "Give me the elephant." Simran put both hands on the box. "No. You never give me blocks." Babloo stamped his foot. The creche didi sat down. "Babloo, what could you share?" Babloo looked at his mat, then pushed two blocks over.

qa.q: What did Kiran give Simran yesterday?
qa.a: Kiran gave her the red crayon when she was colouring an apple.

qa.q: Why did Simran put both hands on the box when Babloo asked?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at the unfairness of giving to Babloo, who keeps the blocks under his mat every day and never shares.

qa.q: How did the creche didi help, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked Babloo what he could share, which let him see that giving makes others want to give back.

qa.q: How might Babloo feel when Simran refuses him?
qa.a: Babloo may feel angry and left out at first, which is why he stamps his foot, before realising he could share too.

grounding: A five-year-old shares with a friend who shared before and refuses a child who never shares, showing early 'you did for me, I do for you' fairness.

passage: I'm Charu, Mridul's big sister. On Sunday the building kids played in our hall. Mridul, five, had his new remote car. Guddu asked first. Last week Guddu had let Mridul blow his bubbles for ages. Mridul gave him the remote at once. "You gave me bubbles, so you drive." Then Sonu stuck his hand out. Sonu never lets anyone touch his football. Mridul hid the remote. "No. You don't share, so I don't share." Sonu went red and sat by the door. Mridul kept looking at him. After Guddu's turn he walked over. "Bring your football next time."

qa.q: What had Guddu let Mridul do last week?
qa.a: Guddu had let Mridul blow his bubbles for ages.

qa.q: What might Mridul have been thinking when he kept looking at Sonu?
qa.a: He may have felt a little sorry for Sonu sitting alone, while still believing that sharing should go both ways.

qa.q: Which choice at the end helped, and why?
qa.a: Saying 'Bring your football next time' gave Sonu a way to join the give-and-take instead of being left out for good.

qa.q: How might Sonu feel sitting by the door?
qa.a: Sonu likely feels embarrassed and left out, seeing Guddu enjoy the car while he is refused.

grounding: A five-year-old shares his toy with a friend who shared before and refuses one who never shares, as told by his older sister.
